item.text: {"text":"Mutation testing supports calibrating diagnostics against deliberately injected faults: measure whether probes flag known failures before trusting their guidance. Deep-learning mutation research also highlights stochasticity as a confounder; reversible interventions on one frozen checkpoint avoid retraining variation, although behaviorally ineffective mutations should not count as missed detections. [Probabilistic mutation-testing framework](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2022.107129). Activation patching can test whether restoring clean activations recovers behavior, but localization depends on corruption choices and evaluation metrics; attribution requires robustness checks across interventions. Evidence comes primarily from language models, so transfer to recommendation requires validation. [Activation-patching best practices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042).\n\nFor NextItNet, a suitable calibration protocol would temporarily disable individual dilated-convolution residual branches, inject the incorrect count−1 readout on left-padded histories, and restore each intervention afterward. Its backbone obtains sequence context through causal dilated convolutions; removing explicit positional embeddings is meaningful only if the supplied implementation actually contains them. [NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf). Proposed measurements: fault-detection sensitivity, false alarms under sham interventions, and component-attribution stability across user subsets and fault strengths. Include mixed-length histories to expose readout errors, future-token perturbations to check causality, and clean-activation restoration to test recovery. These are proposed checks, not measured results. Keep one trained model per category, fixed validation users/candidates, and pinned macro validation HR@10 for selection; use score changes and activation statistics only as supplementary diagnostics."}
